items.title: Social Security checks will rise 3.6% in 2027. What the raise is worth, what else changes, and the dates to know
items.summary: The Social Security Administration announced the cost-of-living adjustment on October 14, the day September inflation data came out. It is the biggest raise since 2023, and it arrives with a higher payroll tax cap and new limits for people who work while collecting.

items.title: Holiday airfares are at 10-year highs, and a federal rule starting Oct. 19 narrows what counts as the airline's fault. When to book, and what you are still owed
items.summary: Jet fuel costs and fewer low-cost seats have pushed Thanksgiving and Christmas fares to their highest level in a decade. At the same time, a Department of Transportation rule taking effect October 19 changes how ten kinds of disruptions are classified, which can affect the meals and hotels airlines offer when things go wrong.

items.title: ACA open enrollment starts Nov. 1 with premiums up again and no enhanced subsidies. The deadlines, the numbers and what to check before you renew
items.summary: Proposed 2027 marketplace premiums are up about 15% at the median, and the extra federal subsidies that cushioned buyers through 2025 are gone. A court fight over the enrollment calendar is still on appeal. Here is what shoppers, the self-employed and small employers should know.

items.title: Shipping small orders to Europe this holiday season now costs more. The EU's €3 parcel duty, the €2 handling fee due Nov. 1, and what sellers outside the bloc should do
items.summary: Europe ended duty-free treatment for parcels worth up to €150 this summer. Two more changes are scheduled for November 1, just as holiday orders start shipping. Here is how the charges stack up on a typical order, and who actually pays them.

items.title: Apple's smart home push: HomeView, a $299 Apple TV, a new HomePod mini and its own cameras and locks. What was announced, what it costs and what to know first
items.summary: At its October 13 event, Apple introduced a seven-inch home hub, a new Apple TV and HomePod mini, and a line of cameras, locks and thermostats built with LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. The common thread is Siri AI, which is still in beta and not available in the European Union.

items.title: Nearly one in three Denver listings cut its price in September, the second-highest share among big metros. What the record price cuts mean for buyers and sellers
items.summary: Nationally, 20.8% of homes for sale had a price reduction in September, the highest share for the month in Realtor.com's records. Denver's share was 32.1%, behind only Salt Lake City. Inventory is close to pre-pandemic levels, but higher mortgage rates are limiting how many buyers can take advantage.

items.title: New SBA loan rules took effect Oct. 1. Buying a small business with a 7(a) loan now takes more cash, more proof and a citizenship check
items.summary: The Small Business Administration's updated lending rulebook applies to every 7(a) and 504 loan numbered on or after October 1. The biggest changes land on people buying, expanding or buying out a business, and they are easier to plan around before a letter of intent than after.

items.title: New York City's click-to-cancel rule is now in force, and the federal rule is still dead. A compliance map for any business that sells subscriptions
items.summary: With the FTC's nationwide rule vacated in 2025, subscription law is now written city by city and state by state. New York City's rule, which took effect October 1, is the most detailed yet, and it reaches businesses that serve New Yorkers wherever the business is based.

items.title: Colorado ballots are in mailboxes. The deadlines that matter before Nov. 3, and a plain-language list of all 14 statewide measures
items.summary: County clerks had until October 9 to mail ballots to every active registered voter, and drop boxes opened October 12. The ballot is long this year, with seven constitutional amendments, seven statutory propositions and a regional rail tax in parts of 13 counties.

items.title: This year's Antarctic ozone hole was the second-largest on record for its time of year. Scientists say the ozone layer is still healing. Here is how both can be true
items.summary: Satellite data from Europe's Copernicus service show the hole opened early and grew to roughly 27.4 million square kilometers by September 20, close to the 2015 record for that time of year. Atmospheric scientists attribute the size mostly to an unusually strong, cold polar vortex rather than more ozone-destroying chemicals.

items.title: Eye To Ad Media's fall launches: an AI agent factory, a member-controlled social network and a press release network. What each does, what it costs and who it suits
items.summary: The Denver marketing firm, which shares ownership with Action Global News, is rolling out several products this fall. This overview sets out what each one does, the published prices, who it is meant for and what a small business owner should check before signing up.

items.title: A free referral network opens seats in Denver, Colorado Springs and Fort Collins, with a 45-minute weekly format and no dues
items.summary: NexGen Lead Groups, a referral network operated by the publisher of this site, began accepting members on October 14 for its first three Colorado groups. Here is how the format works, and how any owner can judge whether a referral group is worth the hour.

items.title: Colorado voters face two income tax measures written to collide. What Amendment 87 and Proposition 136 would mean for households and business owners
items.summary: A graduated income tax that would cut rates for most filers and nearly double the top rate is on the Nov. 3 ballot alongside a measure to cap the flat 4.4% rate. The governor has weighed in, and outside money is pouring in.

items.title: Big banks opened earnings season with rising loans and lower card losses. Their CEOs are bracing for higher rates anyway
items.summary: JPMorgan, Wells Fargo, Citi, Goldman Sachs and Bank of America reported higher loan balances and mostly steady credit in the third quarter. Executives still flagged rates, oil and inflation as risks, and JPMorgan is tightening credit slightly.

items.title: Prime Big Deal Days drew $9.86 billion online. Now the holiday shipping surcharges and fee changes arrive for sellers
items.summary: October's Amazon deal event grew 8.5% as shoppers chased low-priced basics. Holiday forecasts point to steady online growth, but carrier surcharges, platform fee changes and hotter inflation will decide how much of it sellers keep.

items.title: Inflation hit 3.7% in September as gas jumped 9%. The hotter core number is what puts another Fed hike in play
items.summary: Consumer prices rose 3.7% over the past year, led by a 9.1% monthly jump in gasoline. Core inflation also beat forecasts, lifting the odds of a second Federal Reserve rate increase on October 28.

items.title: Federal agents raided more than 40 North Korean laptop farms in Texas. The FBI says employers hiring remote workers are the front line
items.summary: An Ohio indictment and Texas raids exposed a scheme that put North Korean operatives on the payrolls of more than 70 U.S. companies. The FBI's new alert explains how the scheme is changing and how employers can check their own remote hires.

items.title: The first real storm hits Colorado's ski country, and Keystone is already selling tickets for Oct. 24. Where the race to open stands after a record-bad winter
items.summary: Colorado's high country is getting its first significant snow of the season as resorts wait for cold enough nights to make snow. After a winter with the lowest skier visits since 1991-92, the timing of opening day carries extra weight.

items.title: Mortgage rates hit 7.4% and pending home sales fell to their lowest since 2014. Here is what the slowdown means for buyers, sellers and Denver
items.summary: The 30-year mortgage rate reached 7.40%, its highest since November 2023, and new contracts fell to a 12-year low in September. Existing-home sales rose slightly, but NAR expects fourth-quarter closings to drop.

items.title: Congo's Ebola outbreak has passed 9,000 confirmed cases, and there is still no approved vaccine for this strain. Where it stands
items.summary: The Bundibugyo virus outbreak is now the largest in Congo's history and second only to West Africa's 2014–2016 epidemic. Conflict, mistrust and shortages are slowing the response, while vaccine trials are still being prepared.

items.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon reached paying subscribers this week. What businesses get, what it costs, and when the price doubles
items.summary: Google opened its new frontier model to AI Pro and Ultra subscribers and API customers on October 13. Here is who can use it, what it costs, what Google disclosed about its flaws, and how to test it.

items.title: Denver's airport now reads your license plate and skips the parking kiosk. What Express Pay changes, and what else to know before flying out of DEN this fall
items.summary: Denver International Airport rolled out license plate-based parking payments in the middle of a fall break rush TSA expects to top 965,000 passengers. Here is how to enroll, what parking costs and how ID and PreCheck rules are shifting.

items.title: The IMF lifted its 2026 world growth forecast to 3.1%, but says only 32 economies are doing most of the growing
items.summary: Released at the Annual Meetings in Bangkok, the IMF's October outlook says AI investment is offsetting a war-driven energy shock, but the gains are concentrated and inflation is running higher than expected.

items.title: The economics Nobel goes to Robert Hall and Michael Woodford, whose models taught central banks to steer with expectations
items.summary: The Stanford and Columbia economists share the 12 million kronor prize for grounding economic stabilization policy in how households and firms actually decide, an approach behind modern forward guidance.

items.title: Meta's Connect 2026 put glasses first and pushed its next VR device to 2027. What was announced, and what it costs
items.summary: The company that sells most of the world's smart glasses used its annual developer conference to widen that lead: a cheaper audio-only pair, a pricier third generation of its camera glasses, a hearing-assistance feature, and a tethered VR device that will not arrive until next spring.

items.title: Smart glasses are now most of the XR market. The latest shipment data shows how fast headsets lost ground
items.summary: For a decade, virtual and augmented reality meant a headset. The latest quarterly figures from IDC show glasses, most without full displays, now account for the large majority of devices shipped, and one company accounts for most of those.

items.title: The arts endowment's budget is in limbo again. What the fiscal 2027 fight means for local arts groups
items.summary: The federal government's main arts grant-maker starts another fiscal year without a final budget. The White House wants to wind it down, a House committee would cut it by about a third, and the Senate has not yet acted. Much of the money reaches communities through state arts agencies.

items.title: Global art sales grew again in 2025, to $59.6 billion. The recovery was real, and very uneven
items.summary: After two down years, the art trade grew in 2025. Public auctions and works above $10 million did most of the lifting, art fairs took a bigger share of dealer sales, and the middle of the market is still waiting for its turn.

items.title: Outdoor recreation is a $700 billion slice of the U.S. economy. The latest federal numbers, and what they mean in Colorado
items.summary: The government's outdoor recreation account counts everything from boat sales to guided trips and the hotels that house the people taking them. Its 2024 edition shows an industry still growing, more slowly, and paying its workers more.

items.title: Colorado now counts 45 wolves, but no new releases are coming this winter. Where the reintroduction stands
items.summary: Nearly three years after voters' wolves first touched Colorado soil, the state's population is larger than ever and more fragile than officials hoped. Releases are on hold, adult survival is below normal, and the rules for wolves that kill livestock are being rewritten.

items.title: Front Range voters will decide whether to tax themselves for a train to Pueblo. What Issue 7A would buy
items.summary: A first phase of trains between Denver and Fort Collins is already funded for 2029. Issue 7A would pay for more frequent service and an extension south to Pueblo. A ballot mix-up means hundreds of thousands of people received a question they cannot vote on.

items.title: U.S. measles cases passed 4,000 this year. In November, health officials decide whether the country is still measles-free
items.summary: The United States declared measles eliminated in 2000. A record year of outbreaks, linked chains of transmission dating to January 2025, and a regional review next month could end that status. The protection available to families has not changed.

items.title: Europe's border check now takes your fingerprints. The travel authorization is still coming. What Americans need to know
items.summary: Visitors from outside the EU are now registered with a face scan and fingerprints on their first trip into the Schengen area. The separate online travel authorization, ETIAS, has slipped again. Here is what applies now, what does not, and how to avoid the worst queues.

items.title: International visitors now pay $100 extra at 11 national parks, including Rocky Mountain. How the fee works
items.summary: The surcharge applies at the parks that draw the most foreign visitors, from Yellowstone to Rocky Mountain. For travelers it changes the math of a road trip. For gateway towns that depend on international guests, it adds a cost at the entrance.

items.title: Medicare open enrollment starts October 15. The drug cap is rising, some prices are falling, and your plan may have changed
items.summary: For 2027 the most anyone pays out of pocket for covered Part D drugs goes up by $300, while negotiated prices take effect on a second group of drugs, including semaglutide. The only way to know what it means for you is to compare plans.

items.title: The 1099 threshold is now $2,000 and bonus depreciation is back at 100%. A year-end checklist for owners
items.summary: Two changes from last year's federal tax law land on small businesses this filing season: fewer contractor forms, and an immediate write-off for most equipment. Neither happens automatically in your software, and one depends on what you put in service before the year ends.

items.title: The Supreme Court struck down the emergency tariffs. Getting the money back is a separate fight
items.summary: Roughly $166 billion in duties was collected under the emergency-powers tariffs the Court invalidated in February. Refunds depend on filing, on the status of each entry, and on an appeal that is still running. Small importers have the most to lose by waiting.

items.title: The Fed raised rates for the first time since 2023. What a quarter point means for small business borrowing
items.summary: A unanimous vote, a new chair's first hike, and a signal that one more is likely before year-end. For businesses that borrow on variable rates, the effect shows up quickly. For those with fixed-rate debt, the bigger question is what comes next.

items.title: Colorado scrapped its landmark AI law and wrote a narrower one. Here is what businesses will owe consumers in 2027
items.summary: The 2024 Colorado AI Act never took effect. Its replacement drops impact assessments and the duty of care, and focuses instead on telling people when software helped decide their loan, lease or job, and letting them push back.

items.title: Europe delayed its high-risk AI rules. The transparency rules arrived on schedule anyway
items.summary: The Digital Omnibus on AI moved the hardest compliance deadlines by more than a year. It left the obligations themselves in place, and it did not touch the disclosure duties that now apply to chatbots, deepfakes and AI-generated text.

items.title: Home users got another free year of Windows 10 security updates. Businesses did not. Here is the difference
items.summary: Year one of Windows 10's paid safety net ends October 13. Microsoft quietly gave home PCs a free extension; company-managed machines move to a price that doubles. Many small businesses sit awkwardly between the two.

items.title: COP31 opens in Antalya next month with two presidencies and an unfinished fight over fossil fuels
items.summary: Türkiye hosts, Australia runs the talks, and the Pacific gets a pre-summit stage. Behind the unusual arrangement sit the same questions Belém left open: how to plan an exit from fossil fuels, and who pays for adaptation.

items.title: The Peace Prize goes to Navi Pillay. The committee says the real subject is international law under strain
items.summary: A South African lawyer who sat on the Rwanda tribunal and the International Criminal Court, then led the UN's human rights office, is this year's laureate. The Norwegian Nobel Committee framed the choice as a message about the international legal system itself.

items.title: A telescope made of Antarctic ice wins the physics Nobel. What IceCube found, and why neutrinos matter
items.summary: Neutrinos pass through almost everything, which makes them hard to catch and valuable once caught. Francis Halzen spent decades arguing that a cubic kilometer of polar ice could catch them. This year's prize says he was right.

items.title: The medicine Nobel rewards a way to switch brain cells on with light. Here is how optogenetics works
items.summary: A protein that lets pond algae steer toward sunlight became one of neuroscience's most widely used tools. Three scientists who turned it into a switch for nerve cells share this year's prize in physiology or medicine.

items.title: Monitored wildlife populations are down 73% since 1970. This year’s report leans on the recoveries
items.summary: The headline figure matches the last edition, now extended to 2022. The emphasis has shifted: WWF wants readers to see that targeted conservation is working, and that energy, food and finance decide the rest.

items.title: WHO’s first global rules for treating childhood obesity put lifestyle first and limit drugs to teens
items.summary: About 170 million children and adolescents were living with obesity in 2024. The new guidance treats obesity as a chronic disease, leads with structured lifestyle programs, and draws a firm line on medicines for younger children.

items.title: The chemistry Nobel goes to the scientists who showed how molecules pick a side
items.summary: Many molecules come in left- and right-handed forms, and life uses only one. Two chemists, working a decade apart, showed how a tiny imbalance between those forms can be amplified, work now used in designing reactions for drug manufacturing.

items.title: Samsung’s quarterly profit just topped 100 trillion won. The AI memory boom paid for it
items.summary: Preliminary figures show operating profit up 783% from a year earlier on surging demand for the memory that AI data centers run on. The same price spike is quietly raising costs elsewhere.

items.title: Free AI agents are everywhere now. When does a business need one built to fit?
items.summary: The platforms are giving away general-purpose agents. The work that actually saves a small business time usually lives in the gaps between its own systems, and that is where custom builds earn their keep.
